cards.title: Evaluate Offers by Profit Per Session
cards.summary: Test offers against Profit Per Session (net profit ÷ sessions) rather than AOV or revenue alone.
cards.use_when: Choosing between offer variants (discount depth, bundle size, free-gift structure) and you need a decision rule that protects margin.
steps: Define Profit Per Session = Total Net Profit ÷ Total Sessions, and track it per offer variant, not just store-wide.
Recognise that conversion rate and AOV both feed this metric, and both are influenced by creative, traffic source and site as well as the offer — so isolate offer changes where you can.
Before testing a higher-AOV offer, model the expected conversion-rate drop: a forced pack (e.g. a 360-day supply) can raise AOV while dropping conversion enough that profit per visitor falls.
Run the offer test against a control that keeps creative constant if you want to attribute the result to the offer; test offers and creatives in parallel once you have a working baseline.
Judge the winner on net profit per session, not on revenue: a variant can post higher revenue and still lose money if profit targets weren't adjusted.
caveats: The source warns that a merchant running a 'buy two get one free' offer scaled revenue but lost profit because profit targets weren't recalculated — revenue growth is not evidence of a winning offer.
There is no universal winning structure; the source explicitly rejects any 'magic formula' offer and says it must be tested per brand.

cards.title: Model Fixed Costs Across Bundle Tiers Before Discounting
cards.summary: Build a simple cost/shipping/margin spreadsheet per offer tier so bundle depth is funded by real operational savings.
cards.use_when: Designing multi-pack or bundle tiers and deciding how deep a discount the economics can support.
steps: List per tier: unit cost, total shipping and fulfilment cost, pick/pack labour, processing fees, price and resulting margin.

Model shipping as a fixed cost per order rather than per unit — a lightweight item such as skincare that costs about $5 to ship is roughly $5 per unit at one unit but about $1.25 per unit at four units.

Let that per-unit compression plus savings in pick/pack labour and processing fees set your break-even, then size the bundle discount from the operational saving rather than from an arbitrary percentage.
Recompute break-even CPA and target ROAS for the new offer, since a deeper bundle changes both margin and cost structure.
Round costs up and understate revenue conservatively when modelling, so the offer isn't validated on optimistic inputs.
caveats: The source stresses that this requires knowing real costs in and out and recommends involving an accountant for actual P&L; the spreadsheet exercise is a quick planning tool, not bookkeeping.
Results shown in the source (e.g. AOV moving from $93 to $135) are examples from other stores, not benchmarks for any given brand.

cards.title: Balance AOV Against Conversion Rate Instead of Chasing AOV
cards.summary: Treat AOV and conversion rate as a trade-off to be optimised jointly, not a one-directional push for bigger orders.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add larger packs, raise prices, or restrict selection to higher-ticket options.
steps: Do not simply offer the most expensive option or assume the highest AOV variant wins — offering only a year's supply, for instance, can cut conversion because few buyers want that quantity.
Compare variants on profit per session: a lower-AOV offer with materially higher conversion can beat a higher-AOV offer that suppresses conversion.
Keep at least one low-friction entry option available if your audience isn't uniformly ready for bulk purchasing.
Where you add tiers, keep the entry tier's promise intact so the added tiers read as upgrades rather than as the only sensible choice.
Re-test the balance after changing traffic source or creative, because a different audience (e.g. buying for a family rather than for themselves) shifts both AOV and conversion.
caveats: The source presents this as a general balancing act, not a formula with a target ratio; the correct point depends on your own margins and audience.

cards.title: Use the Rule of Larger Numbers for Discount Framing
cards.summary: Display the discount as whichever is numerically larger — dollars saved or percentage off — to reduce hesitation.
cards.use_when: Writing discount badges, offer headlines and bundle callouts, and choosing between '$ off' and '% off' copy.
steps: Calculate both representations for each offer: absolute dollars saved and percentage off.
Show whichever number is larger — the source's example: '$178 Saved' beats '10% Off', while '61% Off' beats '$40 Saved'.
Apply the same logic to bundle tier labels, so the saving displayed against each tier is the more impressive of the two numbers.
Keep the displayed figure honest and consistent with the actual saving at checkout.
Test both framings where the numbers are close, since 'larger number' is the source's default rule rather than a proven universal.
caveats: This is attributed to the source as a behavioural framing tactic; it doesn't replace margin analysis — a larger-looking number can still be a deeper discount than you can afford.
No specific lift figures are given; treat it as a copy test hypothesis.

cards.title: Eliminate Buyer Mental Math in Offer Copy
cards.summary: Replace percentage-of-a-unit and multi-item maths with explicit, zero-calculation framings like 'Buy 2, Get 1 Free'.
cards.use_when: Writing bundle and discount copy that currently requires the shopper to compute a per-unit or fractional saving.
steps: Identify any offer described as a fractional or multi-item percentage (e.g. '67% off the 3rd unit') — this forces the buyer to do arithmetic.
Rewrite as a concrete outcome, favouring 'Buy 2, Get 1 Free' over the percentage equivalent because 'free' is easier to grasp than a number.
Convert large totals into unit-of-use framing: cost per day, cost per kit, or cost per unit, so the total doesn't dominate the decision.
Show the saving explicitly against each tier so the buyer doesn't have to subtract prices themselves.
Keep the total number of offer mechanics a shopper has to parse small — simpler value propositions are stated by the source to perform better.
caveats: The source treats this as a consistency heuristic drawn from observing offers, not a tested lift number.
Don't strip so much detail that the actual terms (what's included, per-tier price) become ambiguous.

cards.title: Justify Quantity Tiers With Physical Use Cases
cards.summary: Anchor each bundle tier to a concrete real-world capacity or household need instead of arbitrary volume.
cards.use_when: Designing tiered bundle options and choosing how many packs to offer.
steps: Assign each tier a physical reason to exist rather than a generic 'save more' label — e.g. one unit covers 700 sq ft, two covers 1,400 sq ft; or an individual supply versus a family multi-kit.
Use the customer's own context as the selector: room size for cleaning devices, number of kids for family supplements, household consumption rate for consumables.
Label tiers so the buyer self-selects ('for small living rooms' / 'for large living rooms') instead of doing price-per-unit maths.
Pair each tier with its saving figure using the larger-number framing.
Reiterate the upgrade reason near the tier selector, so a shopper with a higher need actually takes the bigger pack.
caveats: The source gives these as observed examples from brands doing large daily volume; it doesn't claim a specific conversion lift.
Not every product has an intuitive capacity metric — forcing one can confuse rather than clarify.

cards.title: Prefer 'Buy X Get Y Free' Over Equivalent Percentage Off
cards.summary: Frame multi-buy discounts as free units rather than percentage equivalents because 'free' reads more simply.
cards.use_when: Choosing between a stay-even percentage discount and a get-one-free structure for the same economics.
steps: Work out the equivalent structures (e.g. a 60%-style saving versus 'buy two, get one free') and confirm they're economically comparable for your margins.
Default to the free-unit framing where the economics match, since the source reports buyers respond to 'free' more readily than to a percentage.
Keep the mechanic literal and unambiguous: state exactly how many units are bought and how many are added.
Display the per-kit or per-unit cost alongside so the buyer can see the effective price without calculating.
Test the alternative (percentage-off variant) when the numbers don't clearly favour one, as the source says the winner can only be determined by testing.
caveats: This is the source's stated preference, not a guaranteed lift; it explicitly says there is no magic structure and results must be tested per brand.
Free-unit framings affect inventory cost directly — verify margin per order, not just headline appeal.

cards.title: Strengthen Offers With the Four-Part Value Equation
cards.summary: Improve an offer beyond discount structure by raising perceived value across dream outcome, likelihood of achievement, time delay, and effort/sacrifice.
cards.use_when: An offer is already functional but you want more perceived value without discounting deeper.
steps: Dream outcome: align the site and ad with the strongest desire the customer holds, not a bland feature claim — e.g. framing around feeling attractive again rather than simply 'look slimmer'.

Perceived likelihood of achievement: add proof that the outcome is achievable — UGC and unboxing videos, reviews, ingredient breakdowns, guarantees, and demonstration for the actual use case (e.g. parents asking 'will this work for my kid?').
Time delay: shorten the gap between purchase and benefit — faster shipping options, delivery deadlines (why Amazon pushes 'get it before Christmas'), and fewer intermediate steps.

Effort and sacrifice: reduce the work and risk required — try-before-you-buy, guarantees, and buy-now-pay-later options such as Shop Pay, Affirm or Afterpay; contrast a convenience product against the effort of diet and exercise.
Apply these across the whole funnel, from the ad to the landing page, so the claim and the on-site offer reinforce each other.
caveats: The four-factor framing is attributed in the source to Hormozi's value equation; the source says it has reviewed many offers, which is an opinion claim, not measured evidence.
Guarantees and BNPL integrations carry real operational and financial cost — assess them against margin, not just conversion.

cards.title: Match Offer Claims to Awareness Stage (Eugene Schwartz)
cards.summary: Vary the claim and dream outcome by the prospect's awareness stage so ad and page meet the buyer where they are.
cards.use_when: Aligning ad hooks with landing-page claims, or when one message is being used across cold and warm traffic.
steps: Segment by awareness stage: problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware.
For problem-aware buyers, lead with the problem in their terms — e.g. waking with dryness in the morning for a humidifier.
For solution-aware buyers, lead with the outcome category they're already considering — e.g. eliminating seasonal allergies.
For product-aware buyers, lead with comparative specifics — e.g. the easiest humidifier to clean.
Keep the claim consistent from ad to landing page so the buyer who clicked for one promise isn't handed a different one; congruence is the point of this tactic.
Ensure the on-page offer and claims match that stage's dream outcome, not just the discount mechanic.
caveats: Awareness stages and the examples are the source's application of Schwartz's framework; they are illustrative, not validated benchmarks.
Requires knowing your audience's awareness level — the source places avatar and desire research in a separate module, not in offer construction.

cards.title: Treat the Offer as Extending From Ad to Site
cards.summary: The offer is the total package — product, price, bonus, claims, guarantees and conditions — across every touchpoint, not just the on-site buy-X-get-Y.
cards.use_when: Auditing whether ad, landing page and checkout present one coherent value proposition.
steps: Define the offer as everything the customer receives in total and the value they perceive at purchase, including product, price, bonuses, claims, guarantees and conditions.
Map the offer across touchpoints: ad hook, landing-page claims, product page, guarantee and risk reversal, and checkout/payment options.
Check that the same dream outcome and proof appear in the ad and on the page, so interest generated by the ad isn't lost at the buy decision.
Include non-discount components in the offer — free gifts, subscription incentives, proof assets — as alternatives to bundle discounting.
Test full-funnel variations where feasible, since a stronger ad-level offer can improve conversion even when the on-site mechanic is unchanged.
caveats: The source's claim that a strong offer can take a store from unprofitable to profitable is anecdotal from other merchants; no verified unit-margin data is offered.
Ad copy construction and campaign deployment are outside this module's scope.

cards.title: Use Free Gifts and Subscriptions Instead of Bundle Discounts
cards.summary: Some brands grow without bundle-and-save mechanics by optimising opt-ins, subscriptions, and free-gift offers.
cards.use_when: Your economics don't support deep bundle discounts, or your product is consumed on a replenishment cycle.
steps: Assess whether your category suits replenishment; if so, weight the offer toward subscription opt-in rather than one-off bundle depth.
Structure a free-gift or gift-with-purchase offer as the value add instead of deeper unit discounts.
Where you do offer choice, keep it simple: one selection per category rather than a complex mix-and-match builder.
Track the value of the opt-in itself (retention and repeat purchase), since the payoff sits beyond the first order.
Compare this structure against a bundle-and-save variant on profit per session before committing.
caveats: The source notes this brand's revenue level with less certainty than the bundle examples, so treat it as an observed alternative structure, not a superior one.
Subscription value depends on churn and LTV, which the source notes are tracked separately for consumables.

input.source_name: How To Create Winning Offers In Ecom.docx
input.text:
03-OFF / offers Goes here. Pre-purchase offer construction and testing mechanics. The balancing act between Average Order Value (AOV) and conversion rate, tracking Profit Per Session as the core validation metric, cognitive load reduction tactics (mental math elimination, presenting per-day and per-unit breakdowns), contextual quantity framing (tying bundle tiers to physical use cases like room size or family count), the "rule of larger numbers" for dollar-off versus percentage-off display, Buy X Get Y Free framing over percentage equivalents, and full-funnel offer congruence across awareness stages. Not here. • Ad copy construction, account structure, and campaign deployment -> 11-ADC • Avatar objection discovery, desire mining, and customer research -> 02-AVT • Formal landed cost calculations, bookkeeping, and P&L financial statements -> 06-MEA / 20-FIN • Landing page wireframing, layout hierarchy, and visual section design -> 07-LPG

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Enforces evaluating offers via Profit Per Session to prevent margin-destructive AOV chasing, while eliminating buyer mental math through contextual volume justification and the rule-of-larger-numbers discount framing.

modules: [OFF]

topics: [offer mechanics, bundles and AOV, discount depth and margin, guarantees and risk reversal, offer congruence]

tier: 2

scope_hint: growth

Topics. offer mechanics / AOV vs. conversion rate balancing, Profit Per Session optimization, cognitive math elimination, shipping cost absorption across multi-packs; bundles and AOV / contextual tier justification (space/capacity/family sizing), Buy X Get Y Free vs. equivalent percentage off, tiered unit pricing; discount depth and margin / rule of larger numbers ($ off vs. % off framing), cost-per-day breakdown display; guarantees and risk reversal / try-before-you-buy, BNPL financing integrations, proof asset placement (unboxing, UGC, ingredient breakdowns); offer congruence / aligning ad hook desires with on-page claims across Eugene Schwartz awareness stages (problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware).

Look for.

Profit Per Session Optimization: The primary evaluation metric for offer testing:$$\text{Profit Per Session} = \frac{\text{Total Net Profit}}{\text{Total Sessions}}$$Ensuring that an artificial increase in AOV (e.g., forcing a 360-day pack) does not depress conversion rate to the point where net profit per visitor declines.

The Rule of Larger Numbers: Formatting the discount using whichever integer is numerically larger to reduce hesitation (e.g., "$178 Saved" instead of "10% Off", versus "61% Off" instead of "$40 Saved").

Elimination of Mental Math: Replacing fractional or multi-item percentage math (e.g., "67% off the 3rd unit") with explicit, zero-friction framing ("Buy 2, Get 1 Free"), and breaking high total prices into "cost per day" or "cost per kit."

Contextual Quantity Anchoring: Providing explicit physical utility for higher tiers rather than arbitrary volume stacks (e.g., Tier 1 = 700 sq ft, Tier 2 = 1,400 sq ft; or individual supply vs. family multi-kit).

Shipping & Handling Compression: Modeling fixed fulfillment costs across unit thresholds (e.g., shipping a lightweight skincare product costs $5.00 for 1 unit = $5.00/unit, but remains $5.00 for 4 units = $1.25/unit), utilizing the operational savings to fund the bundle discount depth.

Skip. Motivational commentary on "testing more creatives vs. testing offers", unverified revenue claims lacking unit margin data (e.g., "scaling to 100k days in Mexico"), basic instructions to ask an AI or accountant to create a spreadsheet, and promotional pitches for private consulting communities ("Evolve") or courses.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (offer congruence, foundational margin and break-even checks), 85% growth (Profit Per Session testing, contextual tier justifications, behavioral discount framing). Volume. 20 to 30

You can send a million different people to your store, but if your offer isn't compelling, they won't ever buy your product. Most people will tell you just test more creatives, bro, and everything will work out. But that's not true. Offers matter as much as your creatives. I've seen stores double their average order. You can go from unprofitable to crushing it just by having great offers. Your ad gets the click, but your offer needs to close the sale. In this video, I'm going to walk you through the exact step-by-step process to create your first profitable offer, one capable of scaling you to those 100k days. All right, the first thing, what even is an offer in the first place? The long answer is just basically the package of what customer receives in total where the product, the price, the bonus, what they actually getting, how do you make it compelling enough for them to actually feel its perceived value is highest when they purchase basically total what they get, the value they get. That's an offer. Offers are absolutely critical. You pair it with good creatives. Now you're sending at 100K a day. Dude, for example, this dude about this AOV $93 to $135 by steing his customers, improving his offer, did 20K day, up 40%. Let's do the same thing as well. Did 100k day, test two offers, final bidding, one did 100k day in Mexico. All with just testing offers. Assuming even your creative don't change, you can still scale. Now you know what is an offer. How do you create an offer? Good question. So the more important thing for an offers is there's no one size fit all. So what you need to know is your numbers. Always underestimate the numbers and round up because you want to make sure that the end goal for creating a better offer is to make more profit. Right?
